title: V1 resource ownership inventory, v1alpha1
description: Which tool, person, or controller owns the lifecycle of each resource the V1 architecture names, and what happens to that resource under each teardown operation. Ownership means the right to create and destroy. Referencing a resource is not owning it, and no resource in this file has more than one owner. Most rows are design commitments for work that does not exist yet; the v1Status field says which is which, and a row may only cite evidence when it is implemented.

lifecycles.repository: Exists as a file in this repository. Created and removed by a reviewed change.
lifecycles.out-of-band: Created by a person or a system outside this project's automation, on a documented manual step.
lifecycles.external: Published by a third party. This project pins it and can neither create nor destroy it.
lifecycles.host: Belongs to the contributor's own machine. Created and removed by the environment scripts or by the contributor.
lifecycles.operator-provided: Provided by the operator outside InferOps, with a supported provider's own tooling. InferOps selects, verifies and consumes it, and nothing on its platform path creates, enables, resets, reconfigures, or deletes it (ADR 0011).
lifecycles.prerequisite: Provisioned before a workload release and outliving it. Terraform's half of the cluster.
lifecycles.release: Part of one Helm release. Created by install or upgrade, removed by uninstall.
lifecycles.derived: Never declared by any tool. A Kubernetes controller creates it from an owned object and garbage-collects it.
lifecycles.undecided: No owner has been selected. Every resource carrying this lifecycle must be deferred out of V1.

owners.name: This repository and its review process
The team that owns the workload
owners.createdBy: the owning team, by a documented manual step
owners.destroyedBy: the owning team, by a documented manual step

owners.name: The upstream image and model publishers
The contributor's machine, container engine, and environment scripts
owners.createdBy: the environment scripts, or a documented host prerequisite
owners.destroyedBy: the environment scripts, or the contributor

owners.name: The operator who provides the local Kubernetes cluster, with a supported provider's own tooling
owners.createdBy: the operator: the kind CLI, or enabling Kubernetes in Docker Desktop
owners.destroyedBy: cluster teardown, performed by the operator

owners.name: Kubernetes controllers
owners.createdBy: controller reconciliation from an owned object
owners.destroyedBy: controller garbage collection when its owner goes

owners.name: Not selected
owners.createdBy: nothing; no owner has been chosen
owners.destroyedBy: nothing; no owner has been chosen

resources.name: The published WorkloadContract schema, fixtures, and compatibility matrix
resources.handoff: The schema is the input to every other layer and is produced by none of them. A workload owner authors a document against it; validation reads it; Helm values are derived from a validated document. No cluster object may be treated as the source of truth for a field the contract defines.

resources.name: Evidence records under docs/proof/
resources.handoff: A run produces output; a reviewed change turns that output into a record. Nothing in a cluster writes here, and a record is never regenerated by rerunning the thing it describes.

resources.name: A workload contract instance authored by an owning team
resources.createdBy: the owning team, by scaffolding or by hand
resources.handoff: The platform reads it and never writes it back. A field the platform computes belongs in the release, not in the author's document.

resources.name: The secret values a workload's secret references point at
resources.kind: v1/Secret, or an external secret store entry
resources.createdBy: the owning team, or an external secret controller acting for it
resources.destroyedBy: the owning team, or an external secret controller acting for it
resources.handoff: Helm mounts a secret by name and must never template one that carries a literal value. The contract carries a locator, never a value. Nothing in this project creates, rotates, or reads the material itself.

resources.name: The serving runtime image, pinned by digest
resources.handoff: This project pins a digest and can verify what it ran. It cannot keep the image available. A pinned digest that is garbage-collected upstream is an availability failure this architecture does not prevent.

resources.name: The model weight file at its pinned upstream revision
resources.handoff: Pinned by repository revision and per-file content hash. The hash is verified before the file is mounted, because the transport does not establish who served the bytes. The file never enters this repository.

resources.name: The contributor's container engine
resources.createdBy: the contributor, as a documented prerequisite
resources.handoff: Nothing in this project changes host-wide engine settings. The exceptions a contributor performs knowingly are named in ADR 0001 D5.

resources.name: An existing kind cluster, selected explicitly
resources.createdBy: the operator, with the kind CLI or the optional helper
resources.handoff: Terraform and Helm both act inside a cluster neither of them creates, and since ADR 0011 nothing on InferOps's platform path creates or deletes one either: the operator does, with the kind CLI or with scripts/environment/cluster-up.sh and cluster-down.sh, which remain as an optional helper. The environment scripts positively identify it before any mutation -- every node must be a container kind labelled for the cluster -- but only for the one name lib.sh pins, inferops-dev. Deleting it removes every volume's bytes with it, because the helper's node declares no extraMounts. Its evidence is kind evidence and certifies nothing about docker-desktop-cluster.

resources.name: Docker Desktop's Kubernetes cluster, selected explicitly
resources.createdBy: the operator, by enabling Kubernetes in Docker Desktop
resources.handoff: Docker Desktop's own Kubernetes. The operator enables it; InferOps selects it explicitly, verifies it, and consumes it. `implemented` since V1-S3-011: a release was installed, certified, upgraded, rolled back, had a pod replaced under it, and removed through this cluster, and the guard binds each node to a container on this engine and to the API server port the verified kubeconfig dials. Nothing on the platform path creates, enables, resets, reconfigures, or deletes it (ADR 0011), and the cluster was verified again after the teardown to establish that.

resources.name: The project-scoped kubeconfig file
resources.handoff: It holds a client certificate and key, is ignored by version control, and is removed on full teardown. Terraform and Helm read it and must not write to the contributor's default kubeconfig. The kind helper still writes its own copy for the one cluster it creates; separately, inferops::resolve_target in scripts/environment/lib.sh now writes a second one, `.kube/inferops-target.config`, for whichever provider a platform workflow explicitly selects, rewritten fresh on every call and only after that provider's identity checks pass. For Docker Desktop it holds a copy of Docker Desktop's client credential under the same rules.

resources.name: The cached kind node image
resources.createdBy: the container engine, when a kind cluster is first created
resources.handoff: kind only. Retained across cluster teardown by design, so that recreating the cluster does not download it again. Reclaiming it is a separate opt-in step the helper offers, which matters on a host with little free space. It follows the cluster to its operator because it is a by-product of creating one. Docker Desktop's node images belong to the desktop application, and nothing here describes or reclaims them.

resources.name: The InferOps API image built by this project
resources.createdBy: a local build, made visible to the selected cluster by that provider's own image path
resources.destroyedBy: the contributor, or cluster teardown for the loaded copy
resources.handoff: Built and made visible to the cluster rather than pushed to a shared registry during development, per ADR 0001 D5. For kind that is kind load. For Docker Desktop V1-S3-011-PR1 established it: that cluster does not share the local engine's image store, so the image is imported into the node's own containerd and then named by digest there, because containerd resolves a repository@digest reference by name and an import creates only the archive's tag. inferops::target_load_image owns both mechanisms, so no workflow names one. Helm references it by a value and never builds it.

resources.name: The platform namespace
resources.handoff: Terraform creates it; Helm installs into it. Helm must never be invoked with --create-namespace, which is the single most likely way for these two tools to end up owning one object.

resources.name: Shared labels and annotations on the platform namespace
resources.handoff: Namespace-level metadata is Terraform's. Per-object metadata inside a release is Helm's. The lifecycle label that keeps a scoped sweep away from prerequisites is set here.

resources.name: The model weight cache claim
resources.handoff: Terraform provisions an empty claim; a Helm-owned job fills it; the serving Deployment mounts it read-only. Its lifecycle is deliberately longer than a release's, so that uninstalling does not force a re-download of weights whose transport is unauthenticated. The cost is that it holds roughly 1.7 GiB until terraform destroy runs, and that must be documented rather than discovered.

resources.name: A namespace resource quota
resources.handoff: Not in V1. It is named here so that if it is ever added it lands on the prerequisite side of the boundary rather than inside a chart, which is where a quota is usually put by accident.

resources.name: The workload service accounts
resources.handoff: One per workload since V1-S3-004, release-scoped, and granted nothing: the chart renders no Role and no RoleBinding, and no pod mounts a token. Two accounts rather than one because a RoleBinding written for one workload and attached to a shared account is a grant to the other, made by somebody not thinking about the other. Not a prerequisite: an identity that outlives the thing it identifies is a permission nobody is watching.

resources.name: The InferOps API deployment
resources.handoff: Carries the API image, its probes, its resource requests and limits, and its security context. It reaches the serving runtime over the cluster network and never through a shared process or a shared volume.

resources.name: The InferOps API service
resources.handoff: ClusterIP in V1. No ingress controller and no load-balancer implementation is installed in the accepted local cluster, so anything outside the cluster reaches this through an explicit port-forward.

resources.name: The serving runtime deployment
resources.handoff: Separate from the API deployment because model load and process liveness are different questions. Its probe mapping is the one ADR 0002 proved: a startup probe absorbs model load, readiness follows the runtime's own 503-while-loading, and only a socket-level liveness probe may restart the pod.

resources.name: The serving runtime service
resources.handoff: The only address at which the API may reach the runtime. It is internal to the release and is not a public surface.

resources.name: Rendered runtime and API configuration
resources.handoff: Rendered from values that were derived from a validated workload contract. It holds no secret value: a secret reaches a pod by reference to material this project does not own.

resources.name: The model acquisition job
resources.handoff: The one place where a release writes into a prerequisite. A pre-install,pre-upgrade hook, so it completes before the serving runtime's own integrity check runs. It fetches or copies the pinned artifact into the revision-scoped directory the runtime mounts, verifies byte count and SHA-256 before the bytes are used, writes through a temporary file and renames only after verification, and is a no-op when the claim already holds a verified file. An artifact that fails verification is never reused, so a corrupt cache is never a cache hit -- but it is replaced rather than removed first: the replacement is staged beside it and moved over it only once it verifies, so an acquisition that cannot complete leaves the claim exactly as it found it. V1-S3-011-PR2 changed that ordering after the first real run of the upgrade/rollback experiment showed what the old one cost: that experiment's deliberately wrong byte count renders into this hook as well as into the serving runtime, and the hook discarded a 1.83 GB artifact it then could not replace. It writes the claim and does not own it: Terraform creates and destroys that. destroyedBy and survives describe the succeeded object, which deletes itself: Helm removes no hook on uninstall, so hook-succeeded is what keeps it from becoming residue. A run that FAILED is deliberately kept for its logs, and that one does outlive helm uninstall; kubectl delete job -l app.kubernetes.io/component=model-acquisition is its scoped removal.

resources.name: The model acquisition job's service account
resources.handoff: The identity the acquisition hook presents, created by the same hook phase at a lower weight and removed by the same delete policy. It exists because Helm applies a phase's hooks before the release manifest: the runtime account the job used to name does not exist yet when the hook is created, so the API server refuses the Job and the install fails reporting only a pre-install timeout. It is granted nothing and no pod mounts its token. `implemented` since V1-S3-011, with the hook it identifies.

resources.name: The workload network policy
resources.handoff: A default-deny over the release's own pods and one rule each for the API, the runtime, the collector, and the release test, scoped to the release rather than to the namespace so that a Terraform-owned prerequisite beside it is untouched. `implemented` describes the objects: Helm creates and destroys them, and V1-S3-011 observed it doing so. It does **not** describe enforcement, and enforcement is not merely untested -- an executed experiment established that `kindnetd` -- the plugin that experiment tested, and the one both providers' clusters were observed running -- does not enforce one, so the objects are created and inert (DR-04, EX-05). Whether some other cluster's plugin would enforce them is a different question nobody here has asked.

resources.name: Telemetry scrape configuration for the release
resources.handoff: The scrape jobs and recording rules for this release, as a ConfigMap the collector mounts rather than copies. `implemented` since V1-S3-011: a release installed it on the `docker-desktop` provider and the collector loaded it there, discovering and scraping both InferOps jobs. On that provider only.

resources.name: The telemetry collector for a release
resources.kind: platform service (Deployment, Service, ConfigMap, ServiceAccount, Role, RoleBinding)
resources.handoff: The reader for telemetry-scrape-configuration, which was rendered for two sprints with nothing consuming it. ADR 0004 D7 left collector ownership undecided; the Sprint 3 remediation resolved it for the collector alone, as Helm-owned and release-scoped, and left ingress, load balancing, dashboards and alert routing undecided. It reads the scrape jobs and recording rules out of that ConfigMap rather than carrying its own copy, so one release cannot have two scrape configurations. Its series live in an emptyDir and go with the pod: it answers questions about the release running now, and is not a store anything may depend on outliving a restart. V1-S3-011 installed one on the docker-desktop provider: it discovered and scraped both InferOps jobs and a real Prometheus evaluated every accepted correlation expression through it, which is what moved this row to implemented. On that provider only.

resources.name: Replica sets
resources.destroyedBy: controller garbage collection when its deployment goes
resources.handoff: Never templated, never named in a chart, never imported into Terraform state. A tool that adopts a derived object takes ownership of something a controller will keep rewriting.

resources.name: Pods
resources.destroyedBy: controller garbage collection, eviction, or rescheduling
resources.handoff: A pod is disposable by definition, which is why nothing durable may live only inside one. This is the row that makes the model cache a prerequisite rather than an emptyDir.

resources.name: Endpoint slices
resources.destroyedBy: controller garbage collection when its service goes
resources.handoff: Readiness decides membership. This is where a probe mapping stops being a manifest detail and starts deciding whether a request can reach a model that has not finished loading.

resources.name: The persistent volume bound to the model cache claim
resources.createdBy: the storage provisioner, on binding the claim
resources.destroyedBy: the reclaim policy, when the claim goes
resources.handoff: Terraform owns the claim; the provisioner owns the volume. Deleting the volume out from under a claim Terraform believes it owns is the failure this split exists to make visible.

resources.name: Dashboards and an alert routing path
resources.createdBy: nothing; no owner has been chosen
resources.destroyedBy: nothing; no owner has been chosen
resources.handoff: Narrowed by the Sprint 3 remediation. It used to cover the collector too, and the collector is now decided and owned: see telemetry-collector. What is left is genuinely undecided. A dashboard needs somebody to read it and an alert needs a receiver, a routing tree and somebody on the other end, and none of the three has been chosen. This row exists so that the question is answered deliberately rather than by whoever builds the first panel.

resources.name: An ingress controller and a load-balancer implementation
resources.createdBy: nothing; no owner has been chosen
resources.destroyedBy: nothing; no owner has been chosen
resources.handoff: kind ships neither, and installing them was recorded as an open cost; what Docker Desktop provides has not been examined here, and no V1 workflow depends on either provider's answer. Until one is chosen, every service in this architecture is ClusterIP and external access is an explicit port-forward.
